newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany promises "high level" of aid to east.
newsitem.headline: Germany promises "high level" of aid to east.

text.p: The German government decided on Wednesday to continue to pump a "high level" of state aid into the former communist east after existing subsidy plans wind up over the next two years.

Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said that major funding transfers would have to go on after a report showed that, six years after independence, the region had still to overcome the legacy of 40 years of central planning.

German net transfers to the east will total a massive 144 billion marks ($95.54 billion) this year and 138 billion marks in 1997 -- but the burden will not rule Germany out of taking part in the launch of a single European currency in 1999, he said.

"There is no doubt that the federal government will fulfil the Maastricht (treaty's) criteria and that the timetable will hold," Rexrodt told a news conference after a cabinet meeting which broadly agreed to continue the subsidies.

Germany is rowing with the European Commission over awarding state aid to two Volkswagen car plants in the eastern state of Saxony, but the 70-page economics ministry report said there was no alternative to further handouts.
"The federal government will resolutely continue its growth- and jobs-oriented strategy, and above all make available the necessary funds," the report said.
"The debate over the VW Saxony investment project must not become a misplaced and dangerous fundamental struggle between rebuilding the east and unifying Europe," it also said.

Rexrodt argued that Germany's "new states" were undergoing a transition unique in the European Union, justifying continued state aid allowed under Bonn's interpretation of a key clause in the group's founding treaty. Brussels disagrees, and the two sides have taken their cases to court.
Eastern Germany is still beset by high unemployment, unit labour costs over 30 percent higher than in the west and a weak industrial base and infrastructure, the report said.
Huge financial transfers kept one million people off the dole last year, but subsidies will eventually be wound down to restore a level playing field to the European single market.
The report conceded that job creation measures "create no permanent and competitive jobs" and that financial support would be up for discussion in budget talks this autumn.
Rexrodt said the job schemes -- in the sights of Finance Minister Theo Waigel -- would be wound down "carefully".

Waigel has said further spending cuts have to be made on top of 70 billion marks in savings next year as Germany bids to fulfil the Maastricht treaty's ceilings on government borrowing and the budget deficit.
The report also said that after a runaway post-unification construction boom, the base of the east German economy should shift more to the industrial sector.
That would mean more moderate growth -- which is forecast this year at three percent after 5.3 percent last year and 9.9 percent in 1994.

The report also said east Germany was living far beyond its means. The region's gross domestic product makes up only two-thirds of total consumption -- below poorer European Union member states like Portugal and Greece.
It also said that there could be no quick fix for a jump in unit labour costs resulting from a rise in wages towards western levels while labour productivity growth has lagged.
"The greatest obstacle to rapid economic development in eastern Germany remains excessively high unit labour costs," the report said.
